blocks.text: The opening poem moves from youth toward failing strength and death, ending with dust returning to the earth and the spirit returning to God. This fits Qohelet’s wider presentation of death as a common fate that interrupts achievement and remembrance, while time and chance can unsettle the expected connection between skill and outcome.

“Vanity of vanities” (v. 8) uses the image of vapor or breath. Across Ecclesiastes, this image can suggest transience, frustration, enigma, insubstantiality, or an absurd mismatch; it should not be reduced to one fixed meaning in every occurrence.

Verses 8–14 are not simply a continuation of Qohelet’s first-person discourse. The received book has a third-person frame, Qohelet’s extended speech, the closing refrain in verse 8, and a third-person epilogue that commends his teaching before ending with fear of God and judgment. That structure helps readers hear the final verses as the book’s concluding evaluation of Qohelet’s words.

Most critical scholarship dates Ecclesiastes to the Persian or early Hellenistic period because of its late Hebrew features and loanwords. A Hebrew copy known as 4QQoha shows that a Hebrew form of the book circulated by about 175–150 BCE. The book also speaks of God’s enduring action, gifts, hidden work, judgment of injustice, human fear, and final accountability without claiming that people can master the whole of God’s work.
